where: the "Active" checkbox in every row of the Signed-in team list, sitting to the right of the role select
finding: The admin's third named job — switch off the counselor who left in June — is done by hitting a 20 CSS px checkbox that sits 12px from a 44px-tall role select. A tap 8px high or low lands in dead space and nothing happens; a tap 8px left lands on the role select and opens a picker for a different person's permissions. The admin re-aims, and the one action on this screen that removes an adult's access to a roster of minors is also the least reliable thing to hit on it.
evidence: Checkbox is `size-5` = 20×20 CSS px (40px in the 2× frame). The `<label for>` widens the target horizontally to about 75 CSS px total but leaves a 12px dead strip between box and the word "Active" and adds nothing vertically — effective target ≈75×20, versus the 48×48 the brief calls comfortable. Its neighbour, the role `<select>`, is `min-h-11` = 44px tall, so the two adjacent controls differ by more than 2× in height with `gap-3` = 12px between them. Repeated 11 times down the list.
direction: Make access state one target that carries its own label — a full-height pill or switch spanning the same 44px band the role select occupies, with the whole thing tappable and a visible gap of at least 16px from the select. The checkbox-plus-word-label pattern is what is costing the height.

where: the "Active" checkbox and the "Withdraw" button in each of the four Invited rows, bottom of the page
finding: In an invited row the toggle and "Withdraw" sit side by side, 12px apart, both under 44px, and they do opposite-magnitude things: one pauses an invitation, the other destroys it. An admin thumbing down the four outstanding invitations to pause the stale wednesday.volunteer address can withdraw it instead, and the address then has to be retyped from memory — the brief's own warning that the address must be the exact Google account they sign in with makes that a real re-entry cost, not a nuisance.
evidence: "Withdraw" is `min-h-9` = 36 CSS px tall, ~94px wide. The gap from the end of the "Active" label to the button's left edge is `gap-3` = 12 CSS px. Both controls live in a row 104 CSS px tall, and the four rows appear from roughly 2434 CSS px down a 2821px page, i.e. reached mid-scroll rather than aimed at deliberately.
direction: Separate the reversible control from the destructive one — different rows, or push Withdraw behind a per-row overflow so it cannot be reached by a slip. Whatever stays inline needs 44px of height and more than 12px of daylight.

where: the Invite form (Google address field, Role select, Invite button) below the eleven-person list
finding: "Invite the new volunteer who starts Friday" is the admin's most frequent job on this screen and it is the furthest thing on the page from their thumb. They land at the top, scroll past all eleven existing members, and only then reach an empty email field. Every invitation costs two and a half screens of scrolling before any typing starts — and this is the one task that is likely to happen on a phone at all, since it is the one that happens away from a desk when someone volunteers in a corridor.
evidence: The Google address input sits at ~1998 CSS px on a 2821 CSS px page (2.4 viewports of scroll on 844px). The eleven signed-in rows above it are 128 CSS px each = 1408px of list. On desktop the two sections are already side by side via `lg:grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_24rem]`, so this is a phone-only ordering problem.
direction: On phone, put the invite affordance where a thumb is: either the form above the list, or a persistent low-anchored "Invite" that opens the form, with the roster as the scrolling body. The desktop two-column arrangement need not change.

where: the page header, the grey explainer paragraph, and the top of the Signed-in team card
finding: This still reads as the card it was last week, with a settings-card footnote promoted to a full-width preamble. Before an admin sees a single teammate they have read 370 CSS px of prose — 44% of the screen — and only two of eleven people fit in what is left. It is worse for the core member, who cannot invite anyone: the eight-line paragraph explaining how an admin invites somebody occupies 184px of their 844px viewport, above every row, on a screen where they have no controls at all and came to answer one question — who has never signed in.
evidence: Top bar ends at ~48 CSS px; H1 + subtitle run to ~152; the explainer paragraph runs 170→354 and is 8 lines at 390px wide; the first list row starts at ~370. Bottom nav takes the last 64px+, leaving a 410px window for rows that are 128px tall each — 2 complete rows plus a sliver, confirmed in both fold frames. Full page: 2821 CSS px admin, 1783 CSS px core.
direction: The explanation is reference, not instruction — collapse it to a one-line disclosure on phone (it can stay expanded on desktop, where the column is free), and let the roster start in the first screen. The read-only scene has the stronger claim: it should not open with instructions for a task its reader cannot perform.

where: Marcus Webb's row in the Signed-in team list — admin scene versus core scene
finding: The read-only screen tells a core member plainly that Marcus Webb is Suspended, with a red badge. The editable screen — the one where somebody is deciding whether the June departure was actually switched off — says nothing. The only signal is the fill colour of a 20px box whose adjacent word reads "Active" whether the person is active or not. An admin confirming their own change from last week has to compare checkbox fills down a list, and the label actively argues against what the box says.
evidence: `Suspended` appears once in team-core--phone.html and zero times in team--phone.html. In the admin frame Marcus Webb's row is visually identical to Priya Raman's apart from the checkbox swatch; in the core frame he carries a `Suspended` danger badge beside his role. Same person, same data, and the view with the consequences is the one missing the label.
direction: The control should state its state: "Active" / "Suspended" as the toggle's own text, using the same danger token the read-only view already uses, so the word and the colour agree and the row scans without decoding a swatch. This also solves the 20px target if the whole labelled pill becomes the hit area.

where: the "Last seen …" / "Never signed in" line, third line of every row in the Signed-in team list
finding: A core member opens this screen for exactly two facts: who is on the team, and who has never signed in. The second one is rendered in the dimmest, smallest text on the page — dimmer than the email above it, dimmer than the role badge below it. Hannah Boateng's "Never signed in" sits 1514 CSS px down, at 12px and 2.4:1 contrast, so the one line the reader came for is the one they have to stop and squint at, eleven times.
evidence: `text-xs text-ink-600` = 12 CSS px, #475569 on the #0f172a card = 2.4:1 — below 3:1, let alone the 4.5:1 that 12px text needs. It appears 12 times in the file. The email line directly above is ink-500 at 3.8:1, and the role badge below is a filled chip: the visual hierarchy ranks the wanted fact last.
direction: Promote recency to at least ink-400 at 13–14px, and give "Never signed in" a distinct treatment rather than the same grey as "Last seen 3 hours ago" — they are different kinds of fact and only one of them is a to-do.

where: the "Dana Ruiz" account chip in the top bar, and the five-item bottom nav
finding: /team is reached from the account menu, but nothing in the bottom nav is marked current, so the screen reads as being nowhere in the app, and the only route back to the menu that brought you here is a 32px-tall chip in the top-right — the exact corner a one-handed thumb cannot reach. Escape is still easy (any of the five nav items), so this is orientation friction rather than a trap.
evidence: Header chip is `py-1` around a `size-6` avatar = 32 CSS px tall, sitting at roughly x 265–375, y 12–36 CSS. All five bottom-nav items render in ink-500 with no active state. Bottom nav items are `min-h-14` = 56px, which is fine.
direction: Give the screen a visible place — either an active nav state or a back affordance in the header's left half — and let the account chip grow to 44px, since it is now a route and not just a name badge.
